claims.text: The investigated nanoparticles are sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The as-grown AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially have an FCC structure.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
The sluggish-diffusion paradigm fails for AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at sub-5 nm scales.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface energies to drive their segregation to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy gradients override configurational-entropy stabilization in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Above a critical temperature, surface diffusion coefficients exceed bulk diffusion coefficients by orders of magnitude.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-5 nm particles amplifies the surface-energy contribution in the free-energy expression G = G_bulk + gamma A.
Surface-energy gradients create a chemical-potential difference that drives Au and Cu atoms toward the surface.
Au and Cu surface segregation lowers the total Gibbs free energy of the nanoparticles.
Vacancy-mediated surface diffusion bypasses the bulk sluggish-diffusion barrier.
Surface-enriched Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
Evaporation of surface-enriched species causes particle shrinkage.
Surface-area minimization causes the particles to reshape toward spherical geometries.
The critical temperature for sharply increased Au/Cu segregation and evaporation is likely between 600 and 800 K.
Surface-energy gradients alone can reproduce the observed phase separation without invoking bulk sluggish diffusion.
Icosahedral particles have higher surface energy and will degrade faster than truncated-octahedral particles.
High configurational entropy is generally associated with structural stabilization in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed surface-energy mechanism is strictly valid only for nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
In bulk high-entropy alloys, entropy stabilization is sufficient to prevent segregation.
